This video holds two truths at the same time.

First: your fears may come true.
You may be hurt by a man.
You may be hurt by a woman.
Your rights may be threatened by the political party you oppose.
Pain is real, and fear does not arise from nowhere.

Second: you still have a choice in how you respond.
You can act with love.
You can seek to understand rather than dehumanize.
You can recognize that your opponent is not a monster, but a human being who is also afraid.

Most people do not genuinely try to understand those they disagree with. We caricature. We mock. We speak with contempt and call it righteousness. But divisiveness only widens the gap it claims to solve.

Every time we speak with hatred instead of care, we increase the likelihood of creating the very conditions we are trying to prevent. Fear breeds fear. Dehumanization invites retaliation. Ego hardens lines that compassion might have softened.

This is not a “centrist” position. It is only that I am interested in the actions that are most likely to bring about real change, not the ones that merely feel satisfying in the moment. 

I know this is difficult to hold. It feels like I’m shaming you, or telling you that you “shouldn’t” be afraid. I am not. This is a passionate plea to act with love even in the presence of fear. You will never rid yourself of your fear. However, you CAN decide to act with love in spite of it. If you truly care about your cause, you need to learn to act with love in the presence of fear.

Don’t take pride in your hate, even if it’s justified. Don’t identify with your hate, even if you’ve lived with it your whole life. Please: See clearly how it is actually the cause of the conditions you are trying so hard to prevent!

As Martin Luther King Jr. said:
“Hatred will never cease by hatred. Never. Only love can do that.”

I think I’m going to go cry for a while. 🥹

My father was a college professor. Extremely intelligent. A creative genius. He could draw, paint… create anything with his hands. I used to draw and paint too when I was younger.

But I stopped.

I stopped around the same time he stopped coming to get me.

All those years I thought he didn’t want me.I carried that belief quietly into adulthood.

Recently my grandmother told me the truth… and now my heart hurts in a completely different way.

Because all this time he was trying.

And I didn’t know.

So I’m going to start painting again. In his honor.In memory of the man whose mind and creativity live inside of me.

I’m sorry, dad.I didn’t know.

Therapy has opened wounds I didn’t know were still bleeding. I’ve cried more in these past weeks than I have in years.

I’ve forgiven my mother. One day I hope I can forgive myself too.

Growing up without my father hardened parts of me that were supposed to stay soft. It made me colder toward men than I ever realized. 

But healing means telling the truth out loud.

And saying this… finally set something inside me free. #fatherlove #dad #myfather #daddy #daddysgirl

One-night stands are often framed as empowering or empty. The data says neither is reliably true. Satisfaction depends less on the act and more on what happens during it.

What people get wrong is assuming physical attraction drives a good experience. It helps, but it is not the main predictor. Studies consistently show a large orgasm gap in casual encounters, especially between men and women. That gap explains much of the difference in reported satisfaction.

The mechanism is straightforward: partner familiarity, communication, and attention to cues are low in first-time encounters. Without feedback and responsiveness, people default to scripts that prioritize one person’s experience over the other’s. Satisfaction tracks responsiveness, not just desire.

The practical shift is to prioritize mutual feedback over performance. Slow down, pay attention to your partner’s responses, and adjust in real time. Even brief communication increases the odds of a positive experience.

Casual does not mean careless. Satisfaction follows attention.

Once you compare similar roles and conditions, the gap becomes much smaller. This video breaks down the difference between headline numbers and more accurate comparisons. #dating #finance #psychology #mensadvice #facts

Some of the greatest damage in relationships comes from beliefs we were taught to normalize.

Unlearning harmful relationship scripts requires humility, self-awareness, accountability, and a willingness to ask:
“Was this actually healthy, or was it just familiar?”

Not every belief we inherited about love, s*x, gender roles, communication, or partnership deserves to be carried forward. Growth sometimes looks like grieving what you were taught while choosing something healthier anyway.

A good place to start is by paying attention to the beliefs that make connection feel transactional, one-sided, fear-based, or obligation-driven. Then ask yourself:
“Where did I learn this, and is it creating intimacy or damaging it?”

Awareness is the first step. Intention and changed behavior are what transform relationships.
